KEY MESSAGES:

* Winter Weather Advisories Issued: Elevation-based advisories (above
  3,500 feet) are in effect from late Monday night through 
  Tuesday evening for the Southern Clearwater Mountains, Lemhi 
  County, and the Bitterroot/Sapphire Mountains. Additional 
  advisories for Southwest Montana (Butte/Blackfoot region) are 
  likely to be issued on Monday. 

* Heavier Mountain & Pass Snow: Forecast snow amounts have 
  increased across central Idaho and western Montana passes, with 
  the heaviest rates occurring late Monday night through Tuesday 
  morning. Backcountry hunters, truckers, and pass travelers 
  should prepare for slick, snow- covered roads and reduced 
  visibility. 

* Widespread Valley Impacts Tuesday Night: Limited 
  daytime road accumulations are expected in lower valleys 
  Tuesday, before colder air after dark brings widespread wintry 
  travel impacts across Southwest Montana (Powell, Deer Lodge, and
  Silver Bow counties) into Wednesday morning. 

* Late Week Trough and Mountain Snow: After a brief window for
  patchy freezing fog Wednesday night into early Thursday, an
  incoming trough will bring increased cloud cover, which could
  decrease late-week fog potential, along with another round of 
  accumulating mountain snow generally south of I-90 Thursday into
  Friday. 

Through Monday: Lingering valley fog and low stratus will 
continue to improve this afternoon. Mid and high-level cloud cover
streaming in from the southwest should help limit widespread 
dense fog formation tonight, though sheltered valleys may still 
see patchy development. A progression of weak disturbances 
embedded in southwesterly flow will bring isolated to scattered 
light rain showers through Monday, with high snow levels holding 
between 5,000 and 6,000 feet. 

Monday Night through Wednesday Morning (Main Winter System): 
Leaning toward the upper percentiles of the National Blend of 
Models (NBM) alongside recent deterministic guidance, forecast 
precipitation and snowfall totals have been nudged upward, 
particularly across central Idaho, the Bitterroots, and Southwest 
Montana. High temperatures Tuesday have also been trended cooler 
from Lemhi County northeastward under persistent cloud cover and 
precipitation. 

* Timing & Progression: Heavier precipitation rates will develop
  after midnight Monday night across southeast Idaho County, 
  Lemhi County, and Lost Trail Pass, spreading northeastward 
  toward Georgetown Lake and Garrison Junction through late 
  Tuesday morning. 

* Daytime Tuesday vs. Tuesday Night: While snow levels will hover
  around 3,500 to 4,000 feet during the day Tuesday, November 
  solar insolation and mild road temperatures below 4,500 feet 
  will limit daytime road accumulations in lower elevations (such 
  as Gibbonsville, where 2 to 5 inches may accumulate primarily on
  grassy surfaces). However, once the sun sets Tuesday evening, 
  cooling temperatures will allow snow levels to drop to around 
  2,500 feet, resulting in more widespread wintry travel impacts 
  after dark, especially across Powell, Deer Lodge, and Silver Bow
  counties into Wednesday morning. 

* Model Trends & Uncertainty: Today’s deterministic model runs 
  have shifted the primary Tuesday deformation band slightly 
  farther north and west, signaling a 50 to 70 percent probability
  of exceeding 0.50 inches of liquid equivalent through Tuesday 
  afternoon. If this northwest shift verifies, heavier slushy 
  accumulations could extend closer to the Bitterroot Valley 
  (Hamilton/Painted Rocks/Sula) and Seeley Lake, alongside a 
  higher potential for wrap-around snow showers (40 to 50 percent 
  chance of 1 inch or more) reaching into Northwest Montana 
  (Olney, Marion, Glacier region) Tuesday night. 

* Snow accumulations, generally ranging from 4 to 9 inches, will 
  target the higher terrain and passes of central Idaho and the 
  Bitterroot Mountains. Lower passes and higher-elevation valleys 
  in these areas can generally expect 2 to 5 inches of snow. 
  Further east across Southwest Montana (including the I-90 
  corridor near Butte), anticipate a broad 2 to 4 inches; however,
  the bulk of these accumulations may occur after sunset on 
  Tuesday once road temperatures cool sufficiently to support 
  sticking snow. Elsewhere in western Montana valleys, 
  accumulations will largely be limited to an inch or two of 
  slushy snow, primarily on grassy or elevated surfaces. 

* Travel & Backcountry Preparedness: With hunting season still
  active and high-elevation Forest Service roads still accessible,
  recreationists heading into the backcountry should carry tire
  chains, a shovel, and extra cold- weather gear in case heavy,
  wet snow rapidly degrades route conditions. Motorists and
  commercial drivers crossing mountain passes should check Idaho
  or Montana 511 for the latest road conditions, allow extra
